title: Hemoglobin A1c Targets for Glycemic Control With Pharmacologic Therapy for Nonpregnant Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Guidance Statement Update From the American College of Physicians
authors: Qaseem A, Wilt TJ, Kansagara D, Horwitch C, Barry MJ, Forciea MA, et al.
funder: Financial support for the development of this guidance statement comes exclusively from the American College of Physicians operating budget.
authorConflicts: One author reports grants and personal fees from a non-profit outside the submitted work; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. Two committee members were recused from voting on the recommendations, one for an active direct financial conflict and one for an active indirect financial conflict.
result: Four guidance statements: personalise glycaemic goals through a discussion of benefits and harms, patients' preferences, general health and life expectancy, treatment burden and costs; aim for an HbA1c between 7% and 8% in most patients with type 2 diabetes; consider deintensifying pharmacologic therapy in patients who achieve an HbA1c below 6.5%; and treat patients with a life expectancy under 10 years, due to advanced age of 80 years or more, nursing home residence or chronic conditions such as dementia, cancer, end-stage kidney disease or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or congestive heart failure, to minimise symptoms of hyperglycaemia without an HbA1c target, because the harms outweigh the benefits. The College records that other guidelines recommend lower targets on the rationale that intensive control reduces microvascular events over many years, but that the evidence for that reduction is inconsistent and confined to surrogate microvascular endpoints such as progression of proteinuria or receipt of retinal photocoagulation, with no substantial reduction in clinical microvascular events; that no trial shows that targeting an HbA1c below 6.5% improves clinical outcomes while treatment to below that target has substantial harms; and that evidence is insufficient to evaluate targets between 6.5% and 7%. In the ADVANCE trial intensive treatment achieving an HbA1c of 6.5% against 7.3% did not reduce major macrovascular events (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.06), all-cause mortality (0.93, 0.83 to 1.06) or cardiovascular death (0.88, 0.74 to 1.04) over a median 5 years, and reduced combined macrovascular and microvascular events from 20.0% to 18.1% (0.90, 0.82 to 0.98) chiefly through a fall in nephropathy from 5.2% to 4.1%.
